prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map separates the nearby standing person and brick pillars/parapet from the more distant exterior building and ground: across frames 1–4, the person is roughly 0.5–1.5 m in front of the camera wearer, while the opposite building appears several metres away. The person is centered or slightly left of center and partly blocks the window opening; the parapet is below and to the left/right of the person, and the nearest pillar edges are at similar or slightly shorter range. By frame 5, the person appears farther away, roughly 1.5–2.5 m, on the right side near the window, with more of the interior visible between the camera and them. Brightness boundaries make foreground occlusion and relative approach/retreat clearer than RGB alone, but the map lacks a metric scale and shows implausible halos, merged surfaces, and unstable depths around the person's outline, pillars, and bright exterior.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map consistently isolates one nearby person in frames 1–5, confirming that the large foreground region in the first four frames and the smaller right-side figure in frame 5 are the same object category despite changes in scale and viewpoint. The person occupies the center-left to center in frames 1–4, approximately 0.5–1.5 m away, then appears farther ahead and to the right in frame 5, approximately 1.5–2.5 m away; other scene structures such as the brickwork, window, floor, and distant building are not labeled. The mask shows where the person occludes the scene and that parts of the body are cropped by the upper image boundary in early frames, while frame 5 contains a more complete side/back silhouette facing toward the window rather than toward the camera wearer. The small labels for “carrot” in frame 4 and “bowl” in frame 5 do not correspond reliably to clear RGB objects and are likely false detections, while the broken brown masks and changing person colors show unstable instance boundaries.
descriptions.pose: The pose map contains no detected body or hand skeletons in frames 1–4, so it provides no reliable joint-level evidence there even though the RGB and other maps show a nearby person. In frame 5, a small yellow upper-body/arm skeleton appears on the right at the person's location, supporting that the person is farther in front of the camera wearer and turned roughly sideways or away toward the window, not directly facing the camera. The detected joints place the upper body above the bent arm, with the forearm/hand extending down and to the right; no magenta hand skeleton is visible, so hand position and reach are uncertain. This map can reveal limb articulation that is difficult to separate from clothing in RGB, but the missing detections, incomplete skeleton, displaced-looking joints, and absence of legs make estimates of distance, gaze direction, occlusion, and arm's reach unreliable.
